title: Husserl's Project
description: Intentionality, the epoché, and the return to the things themselves

concepts.title: Back to the Things Themselves
concepts.contentHtml:
Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) launched phenomenology with the slogan 'Zu den Sachen selbst!' — 'back to the things themselves'. Against psychologism (the reduction of logic to empirical psychology) and naturalism (the assumption that only the natural-scientific image is real), Husserl proposed a rigorous descriptive science of experience as it is given.

The mistake of modern philosophy, on Husserl's diagnosis, was to start from theories about what experience must be and then squeeze the phenomena to fit. Phenomenology starts the other way: pay attention to how things actually appear to consciousness, with their own structures, before any theoretical reconstruction.

This is not introspective psychology. The phenomenologist studies the essential structures of any possible experience — the invariant features without which experience of that kind could not be experience.

concepts.title: Intentionality
concepts.contentHtml:
Husserl took from his teacher Franz Brentano the thesis that consciousness is always intentional: it is always consciousness of something. There is no bare consciousness floating free; perception is perception of an object, judgement is judgement about something, fear is fear of a danger.

Intentionality has two correlative sides: the noesis (the act of consciousness — perceiving, remembering, doubting) and the noema (the object as it is meant in that act — the perceived-as-such, the remembered-as-such).

This double-sided structure dissolves the modern problem of how an inner mind reaches an outer world. Mind and world are not separate substances awkwardly bridged; they are correlative poles of intentional life. Phenomenology investigates how objects of every kind — physical things, numbers, other minds, values — are constituted in the intentional acts that disclose them.

concepts.title: The Epoché and the Phenomenological Reduction
concepts.contentHtml:
To study how things are given, we must suspend our ordinary commitments to what is given. Husserl calls this move the epoché (a term borrowed from ancient Skepticism, meaning 'suspension').

In daily life we live in the natural attitude: we take the world to exist independently, assume causal explanations, accept scientific theories. The epoché brackets all of this — not by denying it, but by setting it aside to attend to the world purely as it shows up in consciousness.

The further eidetic reduction moves from particular instances to essences. By imaginative variation (asking 'what could change about this perception while it still remained perception?'), we uncover the invariant structures of any experience of that type. Phenomenology becomes a transcendental science of essences — and, in the late Husserl, the science of how meaning is constituted by an intersubjective community of subjects sharing a lifeworld.

title: Heidegger's Being and Time
description: Dasein, being-in-the-world, and the existential analytic

concepts.title: From Husserl to Heidegger
concepts.contentHtml:
Heidegger was Husserl's brilliant assistant and chosen successor at Freiburg. Being and Time (1927) is dedicated to Husserl — but breaks decisively with him.

For Husserl, phenomenology is a transcendental science of consciousness; the epoché brackets the world to study its constitution by pure subjectivity. Heidegger refuses the bracketing. The phenomenon to be described is not consciousness contemplating a world but being-in-the-world as a unitary structure: we are always already engaged, before any contemplative attitude.

Heidegger also reorients phenomenology toward the question of being (the Seinsfrage): not 'what is there?' but 'what does it mean for anything to be?' Phenomenology becomes fundamental ontology.

concepts.title: The Existentials of Dasein
concepts.contentHtml:
Heidegger insists that the categories appropriate to objects (substance, property, relation) cannot describe Dasein. He introduces a new vocabulary of existentials: structural features of human existence as such.

Thrownness (Geworfenheit): we always find ourselves already in a world, with a body, language, history, mood, that we did not choose. Existence has facticity.
Projection (Entwurf): Dasein is always ahead of itself, projecting possibilities, understanding its situation in terms of what it might do.
Fallenness (Verfallen): Dasein typically loses itself in the everyday concerns of das Man, the anonymous public.
Care (Sorge): the unitary structure that gathers thrownness, projection, and fallenness — the basic way Dasein's being is at stake for it.

concepts.title: Truth as Unconcealment
concepts.contentHtml:
Heidegger reinterprets truth as aletheia — the Greek word he reads etymologically as un-forgetting, unconcealment.

The standard correspondence theory says a sentence is true when it agrees with the facts. Heidegger does not deny this; he asks what makes correspondence possible. To say of something that it is thus-and-so, the entity must first show itself. Truth as correspondence presupposes a more basic truth: the disclosure of beings within an open horizon of intelligibility.

This relocates the site of truth from the proposition to the disclosure of being itself. Beings are 'true' (un-hidden) within a world that has been opened up — by language, practices, mood, time. Such a world both reveals and conceals. Every disclosure of beings as one kind of thing forecloses other ways they could show up.

title: Heidegger's Later Thought
description: Language, technology, gelassenheit, and the turn

concepts.title: The Turn
concepts.contentHtml:
After 1930, Heidegger's thinking undergoes what he later called die Kehre — the turn. The starting point shifts from Dasein's analytic to Being itself. Where Being and Time asked how Dasein discloses being, the later work asks how Being addresses Dasein, granting and withdrawing eras of intelligibility.

Heidegger reads the history of philosophy as a series of epochs in which Being is understood differently — as physis for the Greeks, as creation for the medievals, as object of representation for the moderns, as Bestand (standing-reserve) under modern technology. Each epoch reveals while concealing.

Philosophical thinking thus becomes thinking the history of being. The proper attitude is no longer mastery but a meditative attentiveness — receptivity to what gives itself.

concepts.title: The Question Concerning Technology
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1953 essay 'The Question Concerning Technology' offers Heidegger's most influential late analysis. He distinguishes technology as a means (tools we use) from the essence of modern technology, which is not itself technological.

Modern technology is a way of revealing: it discloses everything as standing-reserve (Bestand) — resources to be optimised, stockpiled, deployed. The forest becomes timber-yield; the river becomes hydroelectric potential; even humans become 'human resources'.

This mode of revealing he calls Gestell (enframing). The danger is not that machines might take over; it is that enframing forecloses other ways things could appear. Art, contemplation, friendship, even Being itself recede behind a single frame of efficient ordering.

The 'saving power' grows where the danger is: in the very encounter with enframing we may glimpse that revealing has a history, that other relations to things are possible.

concepts.title: Language and Gelassenheit
concepts.contentHtml:
'Language is the house of Being.' This famous line from the Letter on Humanism (1947) marks the late Heidegger's turn to language and poetry. Language is not primarily a tool we wield to label objects; it is the medium in which beings come to stand as what they are.

Heidegger turns to poets — Hölderlin, Rilke, Trakl — as thinkers of being who manage to speak otherwise than the calculative speech of metaphysics and technology. The thinker's task is not to construct theories but to listen, attending to what language itself calls forth.

The corresponding stance is Gelassenheit — releasement, letting-be. Not passivity, not nihilism, but a posture that 'lets beings be' the beings they are, rather than forcing them into the grid of standing-reserve. In a technological age, gelassenheit is itself a discipline.

title: Merleau-Ponty: The Body-Subject
description: Perception, motor intentionality, and the flesh of the world

concepts.title: Perception and the Primacy of the Body
concepts.contentHtml:
Maurice Merleau-Ponty (1908–1961) made perception and embodiment central. His Phenomenology of Perception (1945) attacks the standard alternatives — empiricism (perception as the assembly of sensations) and intellectualism (perception as judgement on sensory data) — for missing the phenomenon itself.

Perception is not a chain of inner representations; it is the body's direct grip on a meaningful world. Before I 'judge' that the chair is in front of me, my body has already oriented toward it, ready to sit. The body is not an object I have but the body-subject: the medium of my being-in-the-world.

Drawing on Gestalt psychology and case studies of brain-damaged patients (notably Schneider), Merleau-Ponty shows that perception always organises figure against ground, salience against horizon, in ways no associationist model can capture.

concepts.title: Motor Intentionality and the Habit Body
concepts.contentHtml:
Merleau-Ponty develops Husserl's intentionality into motor intentionality. The body's grasp on a world is not first cognitive but practical: my hand 'knows' how to reach for the cup before I form any explicit plan.

This bodily knowing is structured by the habit body: skills, postures, repertoires sedimented through practice. The pianist's fingers know the keyboard; the driver's body knows the dimensions of the car. The body extends to incorporate tools — the blind person's cane is not an external object but a part of touch.

This account dissolves Cartesian dualism. There is no need to bridge an inner mind to an outer body, because the lived body is neither pure thing nor pure thought. It is the natural locus of meaning, the site at which world and self interpenetrate.

concepts.title: The Flesh of the World
concepts.contentHtml:
The unfinished The Visible and the Invisible (published posthumously in 1964) develops Merleau-Ponty's most ambitious concept: the flesh (la chair).

Flesh is not matter and not spirit. It names the common element in which my body and the world are intertwined: I see only because I am visible; I touch only because I am touchable. When my left hand touches my right, I am at once toucher and touched — a reversibility that points to a deeper texture in which subject and object have not yet pulled apart.

The world is of the same flesh as my body. Phenomenology becomes ontology: not a study of how a mind constitutes a world, but a description of the chiasmic, intertwined fabric in which beings show up to each other. This concept influenced ecological thought, feminist phenomenology (Iris Marion Young), and recent debates about embodied cognition.

title: Levinas and the Ethics of the Other
description: The face, infinity over totality, ethics as first philosophy

concepts.title: Beyond Heidegger
concepts.contentHtml:
Emmanuel Levinas (1906–1995), a Lithuanian Jew who introduced phenomenology to France, became its most radical ethical thinker. He revered Husserl and Heidegger but found their thought ultimately unable to reach the Other.

Heidegger's analysis of being-with-others (Mitsein) treats the other Dasein as a structure within my world. Levinas asks: but what about the encounter that interrupts my world? What about the Other whose existence makes a claim on me prior to any project I form?

Levinas was haunted by the catastrophe of European Jewry. A philosophy that begins with my own being, he came to think, cannot account for the ethical demand I undergo when faced with another human being whose suffering exceeds any frame I impose.

concepts.title: The Face
concepts.contentHtml:
Levinas's signature concept is the face (le visage). This is not a phenomenon I observe — its features, its shape — but the way the Other addresses me before I have categorised them. The face says: 'You shall not kill.' Not as a moral rule already adopted, but as an absolute demand that summons me to responsibility.

The face is infinite: it overflows any image or concept I have of it. Every attempt to comprehend the Other reduces them to a theme, a content of my consciousness — but the Other always exceeds. This excess is what Levinas calls infinity, in contrast to the closed circle of the same.

The asymmetry is crucial. I am responsible for the Other before I worry about whether they are responsible for me. Ethics begins with the demand of the Other, not with reciprocal contracts.

concepts.title: Ethics as First Philosophy
concepts.contentHtml:
Totality and Infinity (1961) advances the thesis that ethics is first philosophy — prior to ontology, prior to the question of being.

For Heidegger, ontology asks what it means to be; ethics is a regional inquiry derivative of that. Levinas reverses the priority. The encounter with the Other is more fundamental than any thematising of being, because being itself comes to matter only because there is someone to whom it matters.

The political extension is sketched in Otherwise than Being (1974). The ethical relation is asymmetric, but society also contains a 'third party' — the others of the Other. The transition from ethics to justice requires comparison, weighing, institutions. Levinas does not abandon ethics for politics; he insists that politics must remain answerable to the unsubstitutable demand of the face.
